drills.q: What refactor from Fowler's catalogue targets a Long Method smell?
True or false: a refactor is allowed to change observable behavior as long as the code looks cleaner afterward.
drills.a: False -- behavior preservation is the defining property of a refactor. A behavior-changing change is a rewrite, not a refactor, and needs the corresponding review scrutiny.

drills.q: What percentage of enterprise strangler migrations (2022-2025 analysis) stalled before 90 days without replacing their first monolith component?
Explain Replace Conditional with Polymorphism using a concrete example, and state the payoff for adding a new case later.
drills.a: A switch/if-chain branching on type (e.g. shipping cost by carrier) is replaced with a class hierarchy where each branch becomes a subclass overriding a shared method. Payoff: adding a new carrier becomes adding one new subclass instead of hunting down and editing every scattered switch statement across the codebase.

drills.q: Why does the Strangler Fig pattern require a routing layer specifically, and what does that layer let you do that a big-bang cutover can't?
drills.a: The router (proxy/gateway/flag) decides per-request whether legacy or new code serves it, allowing per-capability cutover and per-capability rollback. A big-bang cutover has no such component -- it's all-or-nothing, so a problem in any part means rolling back the entire system at once.

drills.q: A strangler migration project picks its 'logical' but slow-to-build first capability for architectural cleanliness. Using the 90-day velocity data, explain why this is a mistake.
drills.a: Projects extracting under 5% of monolith functionality in the first 90 days fail 92% of the time -- the mechanism is organizational: an invisible-progress infrastructure phase erodes executive patience before anything ships. The first capability should be chosen for shipping speed and visibility, not architectural elegance.

drills.q: What is a shadow-traffic (dark-launch) verification phase, and what happens if it's skipped?
drills.a: Running the legacy and new implementations in parallel against real traffic and diffing their outputs before cutting the router over. Skipping it means silent divergence is discovered only after cutover, in production, potentially as a customer-facing incident instead of a caught log discrepancy.

drills.q: A migration cuts every capability's router over successfully, but 18 months later the legacy system is still running in production alongside the new one. Diagnose the failure and name the fix.
drills.a: Cutting the router over per capability was mistaken for finishing the migration -- decommissioning the legacy code is a distinct milestone that got skipped once organizational attention moved on. Fix: track decommissioning as its own explicit, separately tracked milestone per capability, not an assumed automatic follow-on to cutover.

drills.q: A refactoring pitch framed as 'the code quality here is bad' keeps getting deprioritized every planning cycle. Reframe it using the principles in this module.
drills.a: Tie the specific, catalogue-named refactor to a specific, already-observed production cost (e.g. three incidents in two months traced to this exact conditional-on-type logic, costing N hours of on-call time each) using the same currency (incident cost, deploy risk) the stakeholder already prioritizes features in -- not an abstract code-quality appeal they can't weigh against a concrete feature request.

drills.q: An org successfully strangler-migrated the highest-visibility 30% of a legacy monolith over 18 months, but the remaining 70% (harder, more tangled, less visible) has stalled for 6 months. Diagnose and propose a path forward.
drills.a: The easy, high-visibility capabilities were deliberately migrated first (per the early-velocity playbook), which means the remaining 70% is disproportionately harder to extract AND harder to fund, since it produces no comparable visible win. The path forward requires reframing the pitch around the concrete, growing cost of running two systems indefinitely (doubled maintenance burden, unmonitored legacy risk) rather than an abstract 'finish the migration' appeal -- and honestly testing whether continuing is even still worth it against that cost.

drills.q: Why doesn't dependency-mapping tooling fully eliminate the risk of a strangler migration's timeline blowing out (a 6-month estimate becoming 18 months)?
drills.a: Static call-graph analysis can surface code-level dependencies more completely than manual reverse-engineering, reducing the volume of surprises -- but legacy systems often have runtime-only coupling (shared database tables with no code reference, timing assumptions, config-driven branching) that static analysis doesn't capture, so real production-like testing still surfaces genuine surprises the tooling couldn't predict.
